{{Short description|Approximation in plasma physics}}
[[File:Picturing the Sun’s Magnetic Field (25513266790).jpg|thumb|The magnetic field in the [[Sun]]'s [[Stellar corona|corona]] is often approximated as a force-free field.]]
In [[plasma physics]], a '''force-free magnetic field''' is a [[magnetic field]] in which the [[Lorentz force]] is equal to zero and the [[magnetic pressure]] greatly exceeds the plasma [[pressure]] such that non-magnetic forces can be neglected. For a force-free field, the [[electric current density]] is either zero or parallel to the magnetic field.

==Definition ==
When a magnetic field is approximated as force-free, all non-magnetic forces are neglected and the [[Lorentz force]] vanishes. For non-magnetic forces to be neglected, it is assumed that the ratio of the plasma [[pressure]] to the [[magnetic pressure]]—the [[Beta (plasma physics)|plasma ''β'']]—is much less than one, i.e., <math>\beta \ll 1</math>. With this assumption, magnetic pressure dominates over plasma pressure such that the latter can be ignored. It is also assumed that the magnetic pressure dominates over other non-magnetic forces, such as [[gravity]], so that these forces can similarly be ignored.

In [[SI]] units, the Lorentz force condition for a static magnetic field <math>\mathbf{B}</math> can be expressed as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B} &= \mathbf{0}, \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} &= 0,
\end{align}</math>
where
<math display="block">\mathbf{j} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}\nabla \times \mathbf{B}</math>
is the [[current density]] and <math>\mu_0</math> is the [[vacuum permeability]]. Alternatively, this can be written as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\left(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}\right) \times \mathbf{B} &= \mathbf{0}, \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} &= 0.
\end{align}</math>
These conditions are fulfilled when the current vanishes or is parallel to the magnetic field.<ref name="wiegelmann21">{{cite journal |last1=Wiegelmann |first1=Thomas |last2=Sakurai |first2=Takashi |title=Solar force-free magnetic fields |journal=Living Reviews in Solar Physics |date=December 2021 |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=1 |doi=10.1007/s41116-020-00027-4 |s2cid=232107294 |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41116-020-00027-4.pdf |access-date=18 May 2022}}</ref>

===Zero current density===
If the current density is identically zero, then the magnetic field is the gradient of a [[magnetic scalar potential]] <math>\phi</math>:
<math display="block">\mathbf{B} = -\nabla\phi.</math>
The substitution of this into <math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0</math> results in [[Laplace's equation]], <math>\nabla^2\phi = 0,</math> which can often be readily solved, depending on the precise boundary conditions. In this case, the field is referred to as a ''potential field'' or ''vacuum magnetic field''.

===Nonzero current density===
If the current density is not zero, then it must be parallel to the magnetic field, i.e., <math>\mu_0 \mathbf{j} = \alpha \mathbf{B}</math> where <math>\alpha</math> is a scalar function known as the ''force-free parameter'' or ''force-free function''. This implies that
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \nabla \times \mathbf{B} &= \alpha\mathbf{B}, \\
 \mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla\alpha &= 0. 
\end{align}</math>
The force-free parameter can be a function of position but must be constant along field lines.

====Linear force-free field====
When the force-free parameter <math>\alpha</math> is constant everywhere, the field is called a ''linear force-free field'' (LFFF). A constant <math>\alpha</math> allows for the derivation of a vector [[Helmholtz equation]]
<math display="block">\nabla^2\mathbf{B} = -\alpha^2 \mathbf{B} </math>
by taking the curl of the nonzero current density equations above.

====Nonlinear force-free field====
When the force-free parameter <math>\alpha</math> depends on position, the field is called a ''nonlinear force-free field'' (NLFFF). In this case, the equations do not possess a general solution, and usually must be solved numerically.<ref name="wiegelmann21" /><ref name="bellan06">{{cite book |last1=Bellan |first1=Paul Murray |title=Fundamentals of plasma physics |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=0521528003}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Parker |first1=E. N. |title=Cosmical Magnetic Fields: Their Origin and Their Activity |date=2019 |publisher=Clarendon Press |location=Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-882996-6}}</ref>{{rp|50-54}}

==Physical examples==
In the [[Sun]]'s upper [[chromosphere]] and lower [[solar corona|corona]], the plasma ''β'' can locally be of order 0.01 or lower allowing for the magnetic field to be approximated as force-free.<ref name="wiegelmann21" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Amari |first1=T. |last2=Aly |first2=J. J. |last3=Luciani |first3=J. F. |last4=Boulmezaoud |first4=T. Z. |last5=Mikic |first5=Z. |title=Reconstructing the Solar Coronal Magnetic Field as a Force-Free Magnetic Field |journal=Solar Physics |date=1997 |volume=174 |pages=129–149 |doi=10.1023/A:1004966830232 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1004966830232 |bibcode=1997SoPh..174..129A|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Low |first1=B. C. |last2=Lou |first2=Y. Q. |title=Modeling Solar Force-Free Magnetic Fields |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=March 1990 |volume=352 |pages=343 |doi=10.1086/168541 |bibcode=1990ApJ...352..343L}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peter |first1=H. |last2=Warnecke |first2=J. |last3=Chitta |first3=L. P. |last4=Cameron |first4=R. H. |title=Limitations of Force-Free Magnetic Field Extrapolations: Revisiting Basic Assumptions |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |date=November 2015 |volume=584 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201527057 |url=https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/abs/2015/12/aa27057-15/aa27057-15.html |bibcode=2015A&A...584A..68P |arxiv=1510.04642}}</ref>
